articles.author: program52
articles.description:
With the new year approaching, a new opportunity awaits - from January 1st, program52 will start posting a different coding challenge every week
The challenges aim to be both fun and educational, primarily aimed at students/beginner/intermediate devs (though those with more experience should hopefully find the challenges engaging too) and will focus on a wide-range of topics including:
science
language
maths
security
encryption
encoding
hashing
graphics
audio
video
games
digital forensics
geography
astronomy
pop culture
...and much more!
It is possible to both play for fun, or, if you want, to check your progress on the global, national or even private leaderboards that you can create for your friends, school, workplace etc
Since there is a challenge every week, people will be playing from all timezones, then anyone who completes the challenge within the first 3 days (72 hours) will be awarded the maximum points of *5000 *- for each subsequent day, the number of points will decrease by 500, stopping at a lower limit of 2500 - meaning that whenever you complete the challenge, you can still move up the leaderboard
Answers will simply be data - strings, numbers, multimedia (images/sound/video) etc, so the challenges can be completed in any programming language that you run locally
You will also be able to submit your syntax-highlighted solution for others to look at in 100s of different programming languages, or a custom language of your choice if your language isn't listed
If you are interested in signing up, we'd love to see you there - creating a community of worldwide developers looking to improve their skills, while having fun doing so!
articles.title: A coding challenge a week - can you complete all 52?

articles.author: Nitin N.
articles.description:
Introduction


Frontend teams often debate Redux vs Jotai vs Zustand.
The real problem is not which library you choose — it’s how hard it is to change later.
This article demonstrates a compile-time state swap pattern using a frontend template I built, validated with a real demo app.
In most projects:
UI components import store-specific hooks
Business logic leaks into reducers or atoms
Changing state libraries means rewriting half the app
That is not scalable.
UI should depend on contracts, not implementations.
In this template:
UI consumes a single useCounter() hook
That hook is the only swap boundary
Redux and Jotai both conform to the same outward shape




{
  count: number
  increment(): void
  decrement(): void
}

No UI changes.
The demo app contains:
One Counter page
One hook boundary
Two implementations:


Redux Toolkit
Jotai
Swapping engines means changing one import, nothing else.
Template Repo: Frontend Foundation Template Kit

State Swap Demo: State Management Swap Demo App







  
  
  Why This Matters in Real Teams


This pattern:
Reduces long-term technical risk
Makes architectural decisions reversible
Allows teams to adopt new libraries safely
Fits enterprise and startup codebases alike
Libraries will change. Frameworks will evolve.
Your architecture must survive those changes.
This template is my attempt to codify that principle. If this resonates, I’d love to hear your thoughts.
Frontend Foundation: A Swap-Friendly Next.js Starter Template
Frontend Foundation: HTTP Swap Demo
articles.title: Swapping Redux and Jotai Without Touching UI: A Production-Grade Frontend Pattern

For decades, software development followed a stable pattern.
You wrote code.
That model is quietly breaking.
Not because developers are writing worse code, but because static code can’t keep up with dynamic systems anymore.
What’s happening now isn’t loud or dramatic.
And once you see it, you can’t unsee it.
Static Code Was Built for a Slower World
Static code made sense when:
requirements changed slowly
systems were predictable
Environments were controlled
teams owned the full stack
feedback loops were long
You could design upfront, ship confidently, and revisit later.
That world no longer exists.
Today, systems operate in environments that are:
constantly changing
data-driven
user-adaptive
interconnected
influenced by real-time signals
Static code struggles in a world that won’t stay sti…

articles.author: Debby McKinney
articles.description:
The first time most teams introduce an LLM gateway, it is for convenience. One endpoint. Multiple providers. Fewer conditionals in application code.
Over time, that gateway becomes something else. It becomes a shared dependency that sits on the critical path of user-facing systems. At that point, the criteria for success change.
This post compares LiteLLM and Bifrost through that lens. Not as competing feature lists, but as systems optimized for different phases of production maturity.
LiteLLM is best understood as an orchestration-first gateway. It provides a broad abstraction over providers and models, exposes many configuration options, and integrates naturally with Python-based stacks.
That makes it a strong choice when:
Teams want fast iteration
Requirements are still fluid
Traffic is…
articles.title: Python-based vs Go-based: What Changes When an LLM Gateway Becomes Infrastructure

articles.author: Debby McKinney
articles.description:
LLM gateways are becoming a standard part of production AI systems. They sit between applications and model providers, handling routing, retries, observability, caching, and policy enforcement. Early on, the gateway is mostly a convenience layer. Later, it becomes infrastructure.
That transition is where many systems struggle.
This post looks at why LLM gateways often hit performance limits sooner than expected, how language choice plays a central role in that behavior, and why we built Bifrost in Go rather than Python. LiteLLM is a useful reference point here because it represents a common and very reasonable set of tradeoffs.
LiteLLM is popular for good reasons. It is written in Python, integrates well with the rest of the Python AI ecosystem, and exposes a large surface area of features…
articles.title: Why LLM Gateways Hit a Performance Wall (And Why Language Choice Matters)
